instruction: This is a new issue for our allotment society. Here are all the articles. Lay them out across as many pages as they need, put the photos I've uploaded where they fit best, and then design the cover: use a photo for it, lead with the best story and add our logo.
paste:
FROM THE CHAIR

Another year on the hill

It has been, by any measure, a strange growing year. The spring was so wet that the lower plots grew watercress whether they had planned to or not, and the summer arrived all at once in the second week of July and stayed just long enough to bolt every lettuce on the site. And yet the harvest table at the September open day was the fullest anyone can remember, which says more about the stubbornness of our plotholders than it does about the weather.

This newsletter is the first we have printed in colour, and the committee hopes it will not be the last. My thanks, as ever, to everyone who kept the paths clear, the gates shut and the water troughs free of frogs.

Rosalind Achebe, Chair

THE GREAT LEEK WEIGH-IN

Nine entrants, one set of kitchen scales, and a result that is still being disputed

The society's annual leek competition has always been a friendly affair, in the sense that the entrants are friends and nobody has ever come to blows. This year tested that description.

The field

Nine plotholders entered, a record, including three first-timers who had been quietly growing their leeks in trenches behind the compost bays since March. The favourite was Des Kowalczyk of plot 22, winner four years running, whose leeks are grown in drainpipes and fed a mixture he describes only as "the usual" and refuses to write down.

The weigh-in

The kitchen scales borrowed from the clubhouse were found, on the morning, to be reading a hundred grams heavy, a fact discovered only after the first four leeks had been weighed. The committee ruled that everything would be weighed again, which took most of the afternoon and a second pot of tea.

The result

When the dust settled, first place went not to Des but to Mira Olsen of plot 7, a first-time entrant, whose leek weighed 2.41 kilograms and was, in the judges' words, "frankly alarming". Des came second by forty grams and has asked for the scales to be sent away for calibration before next year. The committee has agreed, which Des describes as "a start".

NEW FACES ON THE HILL

Five new plotholders joined us this year, and the waiting list has, for the first time in a decade, dropped below twenty names.

The newcomers have taken plots 3, 11, 18, 26 and the long half-plot by the east gate that nobody has wanted since the rhubarb got out of hand. Between them they have already cleared two tonnes of bindweed, built three raised beds and asked more good questions at the monthly meeting than the rest of us put together.

If you see an unfamiliar face on the paths, say hello, and if they ask where the tap is, the honest answer is that it is behind the shed, it sticks, and you have to lift it slightly while you turn it.

AUTUMN JOBS

A reminder of the things the committee asks every plotholder to do before the first frost:

- clear and compost spent summer crops, but leave some seed heads standing for the birds
- lift and store dahlias and tender bulbs before the ground freezes
- clean and oil tools, and bring any borrowed society tools back to the shed
- check that water butts are covered and that overflow pipes point away from the paths
- mulch empty beds with leaf mould or manure from the heap by the north gate

Plot inspections will take place on the first Saturday of November. Plots that look cared for will pass, whatever state the brassicas are in.

SEED SWAP

The winter seed swap will be held in the clubhouse on the last Sunday of January, from ten until midday. Bring seeds you have saved, labelled with the variety and the year, and take home something you have never grown before. Tea and cake will be provided, and the cake, this year, will not contain courgette. That is a promise.
